name: European Electronic Communications Code
evidence_rating: thin on the EECC itself: Commission review and coverage statistics, no causal evaluation; solid older econometric literature on access regulation and investment under the predecessor framework
summary: The telecoms code was forecast to lift EU GDP by 1.45% by 2025 by spurring fibre and 5G investment; that has never been measured. Fast networks did spread - fibre reached 69% of homes and 5G 94% in 2024 - but the Commission's 2026 review found its main investment tool (co-investment) was never used and national rules stayed fragmented, leading it to propose replacing the code with a Digital Networks Act. Older research shows strict access regulation tends to reduce incumbents' network investment.

indicators.objective: The EECC proposal's financial statement has no indicators section; monitoring was assigned to the Digital Scoreboard/DESI, Commission telecom reports and the Eurobarometer household survey

indicators.indicator: Ubiquitous very high capacity (VHC) network coverage and take-up; timely 5G deployment
indicators.target_or_baseline: Gigabit Society 2025 / Digital Decade 2030: gigabit for all, 5G in all populated areas
indicators.evidence: Measured (DESI/Digital Decade): fixed VHCN coverage 82.5% of EU households in 2024, fibre-to-the-premises 69.2% (rural 58.8%); 5G coverage 94.3% (rural 79.6%). Progress is real but cannot be attributed to the EECC; mid-band and standalone 5G lag.
indicators.sources: SWD(2026) 13 Annex 11; State of the Digital Decade 2025

indicators.indicator: Cumulative effect of +1.45% GDP and +0.18% employment by 2025; labour productivity +0.8% 2020-2025
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The Commission's 2026 review gives no macroeconomic evaluation; governments and most industry stakeholders argued the EECC missed its connectivity and investment objectives.

indicators.indicator: More consistent spectrum assignment enabling timely 5G, with total benefits of EUR 146.5bn a year
indicators.evidence: Not measured as such. Review found spectrum assignment delays and high prices in some auctions; benefit not evaluated.

indicators.indicator: Co-investment (Art. 76) and symmetric access (Art. 61(3)) to spur VHCN investment
indicators.evidence: Measured as use: no national regulator formally applied the co-investment provision in five years; symmetric in-building access applied in 8 countries; Commission proposes revising or removing Art. 76.

indicators.indicator: Timely transposition and consistent national rules
indicators.evidence: 24 infringement procedures opened Feb 2021; 10 Member States referred to the Court of Justice in April 2022. Review finds significant national divergence; Commission proposed replacing the Directive with a Digital Networks Act regulation (Jan 2026).

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for a Directive establishing the European Electronic Communications Code and a BEREC Regulation (executive summary SWD(2016) 304), SWD(2016) 303
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for a Directive establishing the European Electronic Communications Code and a BEREC Regulation (executive summary SWD(2016) 304)
literature.headline: If all preferred options implemented by 2020: cumulative +1.45% GDP and +0.18% employment by 2025, labour productivity +0.8% 2020-25; consistent spectrum assignment yields 5G benefits of EUR 146.5bn a year; institutional cost about EUR 208.5m
literature.summary_plain: The Commission forecast that the new telecoms code would lift EU GDP by 1.45% and jobs by 0.18% by 2025 by boosting investment in fast networks and 5G.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Report on the functioning of the European Electronic Communications Code, Directive (EU) 2018/1972, COM(2026) 35 (Council doc. 5633/26)
literature.title: Report on the functioning of the European Electronic Communications Code, Directive (EU) 2018/1972
literature.headline: EECC helped achieve/maintain effective competition and protect end-users, but as a Directive left significant room for national divergence; Art. 76 co-investment never formally applied by any regulator and should be revised or removed; functional separation unused; symmetric access used in 8 countries
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own review found the code kept markets competitive but did little to create a single telecoms market, and its flagship tool to encourage joint fibre investment was never used.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Impact Assessment accompanying the Digital Networks Act proposal, Annex 11: Evaluation of the EECC, BEREC Regulation, Open Internet Regulation and certain aspects of the ePrivacy Directive, SWD(2026) 13, Part 3/3
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Digital Networks Act proposal, Annex 11: Evaluation of the EECC, BEREC Regulation, Open Internet Regulation and certain aspects of the ePrivacy Directive
literature.headline: Fixed VHCN coverage 82.5% of households in 2024, fibre 69.2% (rural 58.8%); 5G 94.3% (rural 79.6%); some governments and most industry stakeholders argued the EECC missed its connectivity and investment objectives; consumers saw wider availability and competitive prices
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's evaluation shows fast networks now reach most homes (fibre 69%), but views split on whether the code helped, and rural areas and advanced 5G still lag.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), EU Electronic Communications Code: Commission refers 10 Member States to the Court of Justice of the EU, Press release IP/22/1975, 6 April 2022
literature.title: EU Electronic Communications Code: Commission refers 10 Member States to the Court of Justice of the EU
literature.headline: 24 infringement procedures opened Feb 2021 after the 21 Dec 2020 deadline; reasoned opinions to 18 Member States; ES, HR, LV, LT, IE, PL, PT, RO, SI, SE referred to the Court
literature.summary_plain: More than a year after the deadline, ten countries still had not transposed the code and were taken to court.

literature.citation: Briglauer, Cambini, Fetzer & Hüschelrath (2017), The European Electronic Communications Code: A critical appraisal with a focus on incentivizing investment in next generation broadband networks, Telecommunications Policy 41(10): 948-961
literature.title: The European Electronic Communications Code: A critical appraisal with a focus on incentivizing investment in next generation broadband networks
literature.headline: EECC generally a step in the right direction, but expected effects on investment incentives, implementation challenges and high complexity of the measures leave substantial room for improvement
literature.summary_plain: Economists reviewing the proposal judged it a step forward but warned its investment tools were too complex - a warning borne out by the non-use of co-investment rules.

literature.citation: Briglauer, Cambini & Grajek (2018), Speeding up the internet: Regulation and investment in the European fiber optic infrastructure, International Journal of Industrial Organization 61: 613-652
literature.title: Speeding up the internet: Regulation and investment in the European fiber optic infrastructure
literature.method: panel econometrics, EU-27 over a decade (pre-EECC framework)
literature.headline: More stringent access regulation of both legacy copper and fibre networks harms fibre investment by incumbent telecom operators, but does not affect cable TV operators
literature.summary_plain: Under the previous rules, tougher access regulation reduced incumbents' fibre investment - the trade-off the EECC tried to address.
literature.period_geography: EU-27, about ten years to mid-2010s

literature.citation: Grajek & Röller (2012), Regulation and Investment in Network Industries: Evidence from European Telecoms, Journal of Law and Economics 55(1): 189-216
literature.title: Regulation and Investment in Network Industries: Evidence from European Telecoms
literature.method: panel econometrics with endogenous regulation (70 fixed-line operators, 20 countries, 10 years)
literature.headline: Access regulation negatively affects both total industry and individual carrier investment; evidence of a regulatory commitment problem
literature.summary_plain: A classic study found that forcing incumbents to open their networks to rivals lowered overall telecom investment in Europe.
